blocks.html: In Grade 6 you learned that a statistical question expects answers that vary. Statistics starts by collecting those answers. Each person, animal or thing we collect data about is an individual, and each characteristic we record about it is a variable. A class survey might record each student's height, favorite sport and number of siblings: three variables.

A categorical variable places each individual into a group or category (eye color, favorite sport, ZIP code). A quantitative variable takes number values that measure or count something, so arithmetic with them makes sense (height in cm, number of siblings).

The type decides what you can do next. With quantitative data you can find a mean, a standard deviation and a histogram, because adding and subtracting the values means something. With categorical data you can only count how many fall in each category and compare those counts or percents. Using the wrong tools gives answers that look like numbers but mean nothing, like "the average eye color."
Ask: would it make sense to find the average? The average height of a class is a useful fact, so height is quantitative. The average favorite sport is nonsense, so favorite sport is categorical.

blocks.q: A store records each customer's ZIP code and the number of items they bought. Classify each.
steps: ZIP codes are written with digits, so they look quantitative.
But ask the average test: the average of 90210 and 10001 is 50105.5, which is not a place and tells you nothing.
A ZIP code only names a region, so it is categorical.
Number of items bought is a count, and the average number of items per customer is useful: quantitative.
blocks.a: ZIP code is categorical; number of items is quantitative.

blocks.html: Calling a variable quantitative just because it is written with digits. ZIP codes, phone numbers, jersey numbers, room numbers and ID numbers are labels: player 24 is not "twice" player 12. Check by imagining the average. If the average is meaningless, the variable is categorical.

Quantitative variables come in two kinds. Discrete ones are counts with gaps between possible values (0, 1, 2 siblings). Continuous ones are measurements that can take any value in a range (a height of 162.37 cm).

blocks.html: A categorical variable sorts individuals into groups, so the first summary is a count for each group. Counts alone can mislead when groups differ in size, so we also turn them into relative frequencies: the fraction or percent of the whole. That is the same skill as finding a percent of a number, run backward.

$$\text{relative frequency} = \dfrac{\text{count in the category}}{\text{total count}}.$$ A bar graph shows one bar per category (counts or percents). A pie chart shows each category as a slice whose angle is that fraction of $360^\circ$. The relative frequencies of all categories add up to 1 (or 100%).

A pie chart works because a circle is one whole. If a category is 30% of the data, its slice must be 30% of the circle: $0.30 \times 360^\circ = 108^\circ$. A bar graph compares categories by height, so its bars should start at 0 and be separated by gaps: the categories are separate groups, not a number scale.

blocks.title: Percents from counts
blocks.q: Of 80 students, 28 ride the bus. What percent is that, and how large is the bus slice of a pie chart?
steps: Relative frequency: $\dfrac{28}{80} = 0.35$.
As a percent: $0.35 \times 100 = 35\%$.
Pie slice: $0.35 \times 360^\circ = 126^\circ$.

blocks.title: Working backward from a slice
blocks.q: In a pie chart of a survey of 300 people, the slice for "Winter" is $72^\circ$. How many people chose winter?
steps: The slice is $\dfrac{72}{360} = 0.2$ of the circle, so 20% chose winter.
Count: $0.2 \times 300 = 60$ people.

blocks.html: Using a histogram for categorical data, or a pie chart for numbers that are not parts of one whole. Histograms need a number line (heights, times); categories get bar graphs. A pie chart only makes sense when every individual lands in exactly one slice, so the slices add to 100%. Check: do the percents add to 100?
To compare two groups of different sizes (say, 80 students at one school and 500 at another), compare relative frequencies, not counts.

blocks.html: A histogram groups quantitative data into equal-width intervals (bins) and draws a bar for each bin, with no gaps between bars because the number line has no gaps. You met it with dot plots in Grade 6 and learned to describe a distribution by its center, spread and shape. Here we make "shape" precise.

Symmetric: the two halves are near mirror images. Skewed right: a long, thin tail stretches toward large values. Skewed left: the long tail stretches toward small values. Unimodal means one peak; bimodal means two clear peaks, often a sign of two different groups mixed together.

blocks.name: stat-chart
blocks.cap: Most commutes are 10 to 40 minutes; a few run past an hour. The tail points right, so the distribution is skewed right.

blocks.html: Skew is named for the tail, because the tail is what pulls on the summaries. A few very large values stretch the right side of the picture out like a tail, even though the bulk of the data sits on the left. So "skewed right" means "stretched to the right," not "most of the data is on the right."

blocks.title: Reading a histogram
steps: Find the peak: the 20–30 minute bin is tallest, and there is only one peak, so the distribution is unimodal.
Compare the sides: on the left the bars drop off within 20 minutes; on the right they trail off slowly out to 70 minutes.
The long tail is on the right.

blocks.title: Predicting a shape from context
blocks.q: What shape would you expect for scores on a very easy quiz worth 10 points?
steps: Most students score near the top: 8, 9 or 10. Scores cannot go above 10, so the data pile up against that wall.
A few students score low, which makes a thin tail stretching toward small values.
The tail points left.

blocks.html: Saying "skewed right" when the big pile of data is on the right. Skew is named for the long tail, not the pile. Check: point to where the bars get short and stretched out. That direction is the name of the skew.

blocks.html: A histogram's shape can change with the bin width. Very wide bins hide detail; very narrow bins make a jagged picture. Statisticians often try a few widths before describing the shape.

blocks.html: You know two measures of center from the mean as a fair share and the median. They answer different questions, and in skewed data they can be far apart.

The mean $\bar{x} = \frac{\sum x}{n}$ is the balance point of the data. The median is the middle value of the sorted data. The median is resistant: a few extreme values barely move it. The mean is not: it is pulled toward a long tail or an outlier.

The mean uses the size of every value. If one value grows by 30, the total grows by 30 and the mean grows by $30/n$, no matter how strange that value is. The median only uses the order of the values: making the largest value even larger does not change which value is in the middle. That is why a few huge incomes raise a town's mean income but leave its median alone.

blocks.title: Mean and median with an outlier
blocks.q: Seven students' commute times, in minutes: $8, 10, 10, 12, 15, 17, 47$. Find the mean and the median.
steps: Median: the values are already sorted; the 4th of 7 values is $12$.
Only one student (17 min) is at or above the mean, because the 47 drags the mean up.

blocks.title: Fixing a typo
blocks.q: The 47 was a typo for 19. What happens to the mean and the median?
steps: The total drops by $47 - 19 = 28$: new total $91$, new mean $91 \div 7 = 13$.
Sorted data: $8, 10, 10, 12, 15, 17, 19$. The middle value is still $12$.
The mean moved 4 minutes; the median did not move at all.

blocks.name: dotplot
blocks.cap: Drag the 47 toward the others. Watch the mean (red triangle) chase it while the median stays put.

blocks.html: Expecting the mean and median to match. They match only for symmetric data. In data skewed right the mean is usually larger than the median, and in data skewed left it is usually smaller. Check by finding both: a big gap is a clue that the data are skewed or have an outlier.

items: Symmetric data: mean and median are close; either is fine.
Skewed data or outliers: report the median as the typical value (and say why).
Need the total, such as total rainfall: the mean times n gives it, the median does not.

blocks.html: A center is only half the story: two classes can have the same mean score while one is tightly bunched and the other spread from 40 to 100. In Grade 6 you measured spread with the mean absolute deviation, the average distance from the mean. The standard deviation is its more powerful cousin, and it needs square roots.

The sample standard deviation is a typical distance of the values from their mean: $$s = \sqrt{\dfrac{\sum (x - \bar{x})^2}{n - 1}}.$$ Its square, $s^2$, is the variance. A larger $s$ means the data are more spread out; $s = 0$ only when every value is the same.

Deviations $x - \bar{x}$ always add up to 0 (the mean is the balance point), so we cannot just average them. Squaring makes them all positive, and squares have algebra that absolute values lack, which makes the standard deviation the measure used throughout statistics. Squaring also changes the units (minutes become square minutes), so the last step takes a square root to return to the original units. We divide by $n - 1$ rather than $n$ because the deviations are measured from $\bar{x}$, which was fit to this same data; that makes them a little too small on average, and $n - 1$ corrects for it. (For a whole population you divide by $N$ and write $\sigma$.)

blocks.title: Step by step
blocks.q: Find $s$ for the data $13, 21, 21, 22, 23$.
steps: Mean: $\bar{x} = 100 \div 5 = 20$.
Deviations: $-7, 1, 1, 2, 3$ (check: they add to 0).
Squares: $49, 1, 1, 4, 9$; their sum is $64$.
Divide by $n - 1 = 4$: $s^2 = 16$.
Square root: $s = \sqrt{16} = 4$.

blocks.title: Variance to standard deviation
blocks.q: A data set has variance $s^2 = 2.25$ square inches. What is its standard deviation, and in what units?
steps: Standard deviation is the square root of the variance: $\sqrt{2.25} = 1.5$.
Taking the square root also undoes the squared units.

blocks.name: dotplot
blocks.cap: The orange lines are the distances from the mean. Drag the 13 closer: the spread shrinks. Add values far from the mean: it grows.

blocks.html: Two common slips. (1) Stopping at the variance: $s^2 = 16$ is not the standard deviation; take the square root to get $s = 4$. (2) Confusing $s$ with the range. The range (max − min $= 10$ here) uses only two values; $s$ uses all of them and is usually much smaller than the range. Check: $s$ should be a "typical distance" from the mean, so it should look like the size of a typical deviation.

In the first example the mean absolute deviation is $(7 + 1 + 1 + 2 + 3)/5 = 2.8$, smaller than $s = 4$. Squaring gives extra weight to the one far value (the 13). For bell-shaped data, about two thirds of the values lie within one standard deviation of the mean.

blocks.html: A box plot is drawn from the five-number summary: minimum, $Q_1$, median, $Q_3$, maximum. Because it is built from medians, it is resistant like the median. Here we add a rule that decides which values are far enough out to call outliers.

$Q_1$ is the median of the lower half of the sorted data and $Q_3$ the median of the upper half (leave out the middle value when $n$ is odd). $\text{IQR} = Q_3 - Q_1$. A value is an outlier if it is below $Q_1 - 1.5 \cdot \text{IQR}$ or above $Q_3 + 1.5 \cdot \text{IQR}$. These two cutoffs are called fences.

The IQR measures the width of the middle half of the data, so it is a resistant yardstick for spread. A value more than one and a half yardsticks beyond the box is unusually far from the bulk of the data. The 1.5 is a convention (from the statistician John Tukey), chosen so that in bell-shaped data only about 0.7% of values get flagged: most flags are worth a second look.

blocks.title: Odd number of values
blocks.q: Find the five-number summary and any outliers: $3, 7, 8, 9, 10, 11, 12, 13, 14, 15, 31$.
steps: The 11 values are sorted. The median is the 6th: $11$.
Lower half (without the 11): $3, 7, 8, 9, 10$, so $Q_1 = 8$. Upper half: $12, 13, 14, 15, 31$, so $Q_3 = 14$.
Only $31$ is outside the fences.
blocks.a: Min 3, $Q_1 = 8$, median 11, $Q_3 = 14$, max 31; the outlier is 31.

blocks.title: Even number of values
steps: Median: average of the 5th and 6th values, $(30 + 31)/2 = 30.5$.
$\text{IQR} = 7$ and $1.5 \times 7 = 10.5$.
Fences: $27 - 10.5 = 16.5$ and $34 + 10.5 = 44.5$. The value $60$ is an outlier.

blocks.name: boxplot
blocks.cap: With fences on, the whisker stops at the last value inside the fence and the outlier gets its own mark. Drag the 31 inward and watch it stop being an outlier.

blocks.html: Two slips to avoid. Using the range instead of the IQR to build the fences (the range includes the outlier itself). And forgetting the lower fence: outliers can be unusually small too. Check: list both fences and compare the smallest and largest values with them.
An outlier is a flag, not a verdict. It may be a typing error, a measurement problem, or the most interesting value in the data. Never delete one without a reason.

blocks.html: Comparing two groups is where statistics starts to answer real questions: Is route A faster than route B? Do two brands of battery last equally long? You now have tools for center, spread and outliers. A good comparison uses all of them, in context.

To compare distributions, describe shape, center and spread (and any outliers) for each group, using comparison words ("higher," "more variable") and the units of the data. Use median and IQR when a group is skewed or has outliers; mean and standard deviation when both are roughly symmetric.

Two groups can share a center and still behave very differently. If both commute routes have a median of 25 minutes but one varies from 20 to 30 and the other from 10 to 60, only the first lets you plan when to leave. Spread tells you how much an individual can differ from the center, and overlap tells you how often a member of the "lower" group beats a member of the "higher" one.

blocks.name: boxplot
blocks.cap: Commute times in minutes over 15 days on each route.

blocks.title: A complete comparison
blocks.q: Use the box plots of 15 commutes on each route: Route A has median 25, $Q_1 = 22$, $Q_3 = 29$ (IQR 7), range 18 to 34. Route B has median 27, $Q_1 = 20$, $Q_3 = 38$ (IQR 18), range 15 to 47. Compare them.
steps: Shape: A is roughly symmetric; B is skewed right (its upper whisker and box half are longer).
Center: B's median is 2 minutes longer (27 versus 25 minutes).
Spread: B is far more variable, with an IQR of 18 minutes versus 7.
Overlap: the boxes overlap a lot, so on many days B is faster. The big difference is predictability, not typical time.
blocks.a: Route A is slightly faster on a typical day and much more consistent.

blocks.title: Using mean and standard deviation
blocks.q: Class 1 has quiz scores with mean 78 and SD 5; Class 2 has mean 74 and SD 12. Both are roughly symmetric. Compare.
steps: Center: Class 1 scored 4 points higher on average.
Spread: Class 2 is more than twice as variable (SD 12 versus 5).
So Class 2 likely has both the lowest scores and some of the highest. A 4-point gap is small compared with Class 2's spread.
blocks.a: Class 1: higher and more consistent; Class 2: lower on average but much more spread out.

blocks.html: Comparing only the centers ("B is higher") and stopping. That ignores spread and overlap, which are often the bigger story. Check your comparison for four words: shape, center, spread, outliers, each with numbers and units.

blocks.html: Is 82 a good score? It depends on the test. A z-score answers by measuring a value against its own distribution, using the mean and the standard deviation as a ruler.

The z-score of a value $x$ is $$z = \dfrac{x - \mu}{\sigma},$$ the number of standard deviations $x$ is from the mean. Positive $z$: above the mean; negative $z$: below. Working backward, $x = \mu + z\sigma$.

Subtracting the mean measures the distance from the center (with a sign that says which side). Dividing by the standard deviation rewrites that distance in "standard deviation units," which have no ordinary units at all. That is what lets you compare a history score with a science score, or a height in inches with a weight in pounds: each becomes "how unusual is this, here?"

blocks.title: Computing z
blocks.q: A test has mean $\mu = 70$ and standard deviation $\sigma = 8$. Find the z-scores of 82 and 62.
steps: $z = \dfrac{82 - 70}{8} = \dfrac{12}{8} = 1.5$: one and a half standard deviations above the mean.
$z = \dfrac{62 - 70}{8} = \dfrac{-8}{8} = -1$: one standard deviation below.

blocks.title: From z back to x
blocks.q: On the same test, what score has $z = -0.5$?

blocks.title: Comparing across scales
blocks.q: Ana scored 82 on a test with mean 70 and SD 8. Ben scored 650 on a test with mean 500 and SD 120. Who did better relative to their own test?
steps: Ana is farther above her mean, in standard deviation units.

blocks.name: normal
blocks.cap: The lower scale counts standard deviations. Drag b to a score and read its z-score; the shaded area is the fraction of scores below it (for bell-shaped data).

blocks.html: Subtracting in the wrong order, $\mu - x$, which flips the sign: a score below the mean would get a positive z. Always compute value minus mean. Check: if $x$ is below the mean, z must be negative.
For bell-shaped data, a z-score also gives a percentile: $z = 1.5$ is above about 93% of the data. You will do this in the normal curve lessons.

blocks.html: Real data often need a change of units: minutes to hours, Celsius to Fahrenheit, or a teacher adding 5 bonus points. You do not need to recompute everything. Shifting and scaling change the summaries in predictable ways, and z-scores are one example.

If every value changes by $y = a + bx$: centers and positions (mean, median, quartiles) become $a + b(\text{old})$. Spreads (standard deviation, IQR, range) are multiplied by $|b|$ and are not affected by adding $a$.

Spread is about distances between values. Adding $a$ to every value slides the whole data set along the number line: every distance stays the same, so the spread stays the same, while every center slides by $a$. Multiplying by $b$ stretches every distance by $|b|$: the deviation $bx - b\bar{x} = b(x - \bar{x})$, so the standard deviation becomes $|b|s$ (never negative).

blocks.name: stat-chart
blocks.cap: The same picture, moved 5 to the right. The gaps between dots, and so the spread, are unchanged.

blocks.title: Adding a constant
blocks.q: Scores have mean 72, median 74, standard deviation 9 and IQR 12. Everyone gets 5 bonus points. Find the new summaries.
steps: Centers move by 5: mean $77$, median $79$.
Spreads do not change: standard deviation $9$, IQR $12$.

blocks.title: Changing units
blocks.q: Heights have mean 65 inches and SD 3 inches. Convert to centimeters ($1 \text{ in} = 2.54 \text{ cm}$).
steps: Every value is multiplied by 2.54.
SD: $3 \times 2.54 = 7.62$ cm (stretched by the same factor).

blocks.title: Both at once
blocks.q: Temperatures have mean $20^\circ$C and SD $5^\circ$C. Use $F = 1.8C + 32$.
steps: SD: only the multiplier matters, $1.8 \times 5 = 9^\circ$F.

blocks.html: Adding the constant to the standard deviation too ("the SD goes from 9 to 14"). Adding 5 to every score moves every score, so nobody gets farther from anybody else. Check: did the change move the data, stretch it, or both? Only stretching changes spread.
Standardizing is a shift and a scale: subtract $\mu$ (the mean becomes 0), then divide by $\sigma$ (the SD becomes 1). That is why z-scores always have mean 0 and standard deviation 1.

blocks.html: Many histograms of real measurements (heights, reaction times, errors in a lab scale) are single, symmetric mounds. The normal curve is a smooth model of that shape. It is described completely by two numbers, its mean $\mu$ (the center) and its standard deviation $\sigma$ (the spread), and it works hand in hand with z-scores.
For a normal distribution, about 68% of values lie within 1 standard deviation of the mean, about 95% within 2, and about 99.7% within 3. This is the 68-95-99.7 rule (the empirical rule).

The area under a density curve is a proportion: the whole area is 1, and the area over an interval is the fraction of values in it. Every normal curve is the same bell, slid to its own mean and stretched by its own $\sigma$. Converting to z-scores undoes the slide and the stretch, so "within 2 standard deviations" covers the same area, about 95%, on every normal curve. (More exactly: 68.27%, 95.45%, 99.73%.)

blocks.cap: Heights of adult men: mean 70 in, SD 3 in. Turn on the 68–95–99.7 bands, then change σ: the bands stretch, but the percents stay the same.

blocks.html: By symmetry, each band splits in half. Between the mean and 1 SD: 34%. Between 1 and 2 SD: $(95 - 68)/2 = 13.5\%$. Between 2 and 3 SD: $(99.7 - 95)/2 = 2.35\%$. Beyond 3 SD on one side: 0.15%.

blocks.title: Within two standard deviations
blocks.q: Men's heights are normal with mean 70 inches and SD 3 inches. About what percent are between 64 and 76 inches?
steps: $64 = 70 - 2(3)$ and $76 = 70 + 2(3)$: two standard deviations on each side.
The rule says about 95%.

blocks.title: A tail
blocks.q: About what percent are taller than 76 inches?
steps: Within 2 SD: 95%, so 5% is outside, split equally between the two tails.

blocks.title: An uneven interval
blocks.q: About what percent are between 67 and 76 inches?
steps: $67$ is at $z = -1$ and $76$ is at $z = 2$.

blocks.html: Applying the rule to data that are not bell-shaped. Incomes, waiting times and house prices are strongly skewed, and for them "within 2 SD" can hold a very different share than 95%. Check the histogram first: the rule is for single, roughly symmetric mounds.

blocks.html: The 68-95-99.7 rule only works at whole numbers of standard deviations. To find the proportion below any value, convert it to a z-score and look up the area under the standard normal curve (mean 0, SD 1). Tables and calculators give that area; the problems here print the table values you need.

$P(X < x) = P\!\left(Z < \frac{x - \mu}{\sigma}\right)$, read from a table of left areas. Then: below = the left area; above = $1 -$ the left area; between = the larger left area minus the smaller one.

Standardizing does not change which values are below which: $x$ is below the cutoff exactly when its z-score is below the cutoff's z-score. So the proportion below $x$ on any normal curve equals the area to the left of $z$ on the standard one. The total area is 1, which is why "above" is the complement of "below." For a smooth curve the single point $x$ has no area, so "below" and "at most" are the same.

blocks.cap: Battery lifetimes: mean 500 hours, SD 50. Switch between Left, Between and Right, and drag a and b; the readout gives the area.

blocks.title: Below a value
blocks.q: Battery lifetimes are normal with mean 500 hours and SD 50. What proportion last less than 560 hours? (A table gives $P(Z < 1.20) = 0.8849$.)
steps: The table gives the left area directly: $0.8849$.

blocks.title: Above a value
blocks.q: What proportion last more than 560 hours?
steps: Same z-score: $1.20$, with left area $0.8849$.
Above is the rest: $1 - 0.8849 = 0.1151$.

blocks.title: Between two values
blocks.q: What proportion last between 450 and 560 hours? ($P(Z < -1.00) = 0.1587$.)
steps: Upper: $z = 1.20$, left area $0.8849$.

blocks.html: Reporting the table's left area when the question asks "more than." The table always gives the area to the left. Check with a quick sketch: shade the region the question asks about. If you shaded the right side, subtract from 1. Also check the size: a value above the mean must have less than half the data above it.
By symmetry, $P(Z > 1.2) = P(Z < -1.2)$. Either way the answer is $0.1151$.

blocks.html: So far you went from a value to an area. Often the question runs the other way: "How long must a battery last to be in the top 5%?" Now you start with an area, find the z-score that cuts it off, and then turn the z-score back into a value, the reverse of finding areas.
To find the value with a given area to its left: (1) look up the z with that left area (inverse normal); (2) undo the z-score: $x = \mu + z\sigma$. For "top $k\%$," use left area $1 - k/100$.

A z-score is a position measured in standard deviations. Reading the table backward tells you that position for the area you want. Since $z = (x - \mu)/\sigma$, solving for $x$ gives $x = \mu + z\sigma$: start at the mean and walk $z$ standard deviations.

blocks.name: normal
blocks.cap: Drag a until the shaded right tail shows 0.05: that value starts the top 5%.

blocks.title: A percentile
blocks.q: Battery lifetimes are normal with mean 500 hours and SD 50. Find the 90th percentile. (The z with 90% to its left is $1.28$.)
steps: The 90th percentile has 90% of the area to its left, so $z = 1.28$.

blocks.title: The top 5%
blocks.q: What lifetime separates the top 5% of batteries from the rest? (The z with 95% to its left is $1.645$.)
steps: Top 5% above means 95% below: left area $0.95$, so $z = 1.645$.

blocks.title: The middle 80%
blocks.q: Which two lifetimes mark off the middle 80%? (The z with 10% to its left is $-1.28$.)
steps: The middle 80% leaves 10% in each tail.
Upper cutoff: by symmetry $z = 1.28$, so $x = 564$.

blocks.html: Looking up the area of the tail you care about instead of the area to the left. For the top 5%, looking up $0.05$ gives $z = -1.645$, a value far below the mean. Check: a "top" cutoff must be above the mean, so its z must be positive.

blocks.html: A scatter plot shows two quantitative variables measured on the same individuals: each dot is one individual, placed at $(x, y)$. In this unit we learn to describe, measure and model the pattern those dots make.

Put the explanatory variable (the one that may explain or predict) on the x-axis and the response variable on the y-axis. Describe a scatterplot by its direction (positive or negative), form (linear or curved), strength (how tightly the dots follow the form) and any unusual features (outliers, clusters).

Direction, form and strength answer the questions we care about: Does y tend to go up or down as x grows? Would a straight line describe the pattern, or would a line miss a bend? How well could knowing x help you predict y? A loose cloud means x tells you little; a tight band means x tells you a lot.

blocks.name: stat-chart
blocks.cap: Used cars of one model: older cars sell for less.

blocks.title: Describing a scatterplot
blocks.q: Describe the relationship between a used car's age and its price in the plot above.
steps: Direction: as age goes up, price goes down, so the association is negative.
Form: the dots fall along a straight line, not a curve: linear.
Strength: the dots stay very close to that line: strong.
Unusual features: none stand out.
blocks.a: A strong, negative, linear association, with no outliers.

blocks.name: stat-chart
blocks.cap: A curved form: fuel economy rises with speed, then falls.

blocks.title: Which variable goes where?
blocks.q: A study asks whether the amount of rain in spring helps predict the summer corn harvest. Which variable goes on the x-axis?
steps: Spring rain could influence the harvest, not the other way around.
So rain is explanatory (x) and harvest is the response (y).
blocks.a: Spring rainfall on the x-axis; harvest on the y-axis.

blocks.html: Calling a curved pattern "no association" because it is not a line. The speed and fuel-economy plot shows a strong relationship; it is just not linear. Always describe the form before judging strength.
"Positive" and "negative" describe direction only. A negative association, such as car age and price, can be just as strong and useful as a positive one.

blocks.html: Words like "strong" and "weak" are vague. The correlation coefficient $r$ puts one number on the direction and strength of a linear pattern in a scatterplot. It is built from z-scores, using each variable's standard deviation.

$$r = \dfrac{1}{n - 1}\sum z_x z_y,$$ the average product of the z-scores. Always $-1 \le r \le 1$. The sign gives the direction; values near $\pm 1$ mean the dots hug a line; values near 0 mean no linear pattern. $r$ has no units.

Split the scatterplot at the point of means $(\bar{x}, \bar{y})$. A dot in the upper right has $z_x > 0$ and $z_y > 0$, so its product is positive; a dot in the lower left has two negatives, also a positive product. Dots in the other two corners give negative products. If most dots sit in the upper-right and lower-left corners, the products add to a large positive number: a positive association. Because z-scores have no units, changing inches to centimeters cannot change $r$, and swapping x and y cannot either.

blocks.name: scatter
blocks.cap: Drag points and watch r in the readout. Try to make r near 0 with the points on a curve.

blocks.title: Computing r by hand
steps: Both variables have $\sum(\text{dev})^2 = 10$, so $s_x = s_y = \sqrt{10/4} \approx 1.58$, and $z_x z_y = \dfrac{(\text{x dev})(\text{y dev})}{2.5}$.
Products of deviations: $4, 0, 0, 2, 2$, so $z_x z_y$: $1.6, 0, 0, 0.8, 0.8$.
blocks.a: $r = 0.8$: a fairly strong positive linear association.

blocks.title: What r does and does not say
blocks.q: For $x = 1, 2, \ldots, 10$ and $y = x^2$, software gives $r \approx 0.97$. Does that mean the relationship is linear?
steps: The points lie exactly on a curve, $y = x^2$, with no scatter at all.
$r$ is high because the curve bends only gently over this range, so a line comes close.
A high $r$ does not prove the form is linear; you must look at the plot (and, soon, the residuals).
blocks.a: No. The relationship is a perfect curve; r only measures how close it is to a line.

blocks.html: Two classic misreadings. (1) Reading $r$ as the slope: $r = 0.8$ does not mean y rises 0.8 per unit of x; slope depends on units, $r$ does not. (2) Calling a strong curved pattern "no relationship" because $r \approx 0$; a U-shaped pattern can have $r$ near 0. Check by looking at the scatterplot every time.

blocks.html: In Algebra 1 you wrote linear models and drew lines of fit by eye. Different people draw different lines. The least-squares regression line is the one line everyone agrees on, and it is built from the correlation and the two standard deviations.

The least-squares line $\hat{y} = a + bx$ makes the sum of squared residuals $\sum (y - \hat{y})^2$ as small as possible. Its slope and intercept are
$$b = r\dfrac{s_y}{s_x}, \qquad a = \bar{y} - b\bar{x}.$$
The line always passes through the point of means $(\bar{x}, \bar{y})$.

Work in z-scores first. A line through the origin $\hat{z}_y = m z_x$ has squared error $$\sum (z_y - m z_x)^2 = \sum z_y^2 - 2m\sum z_x z_y + m^2 \sum z_x^2$$ Each sum of squared z-scores is $n - 1$, and $\sum z_x z_y = (n - 1)r$, so the error is $(n - 1)(1 - 2mr + m^2)$, a parabola in $m$ with its lowest point at $m = r$. So the best line in z-units is $\hat{z}_y = r z_x$: one SD up in x predicts $r$ SDs up in y. Turning z-scores back into x and y gives $b = r s_y/s_x$, and the line goes through $(\bar{x}, \bar{y})$.

blocks.name: scatter
blocks.cap: Each square is a squared residual. Turn on "My own line" and try to make the total area smaller than the least-squares line's. You can't.

blocks.title: Building the line from summaries
blocks.q: For students' study hours (x) and scores (y): $\bar{x} = 6$, $s_x = 2$, $\bar{y} = 75$, $s_y = 10$, $r = 0.6$. Find the least-squares line and predict the score for 8 hours.
steps: Slope: $b = 0.6 \cdot \dfrac{10}{2} = 3$ points per hour.
Intercept: $a = 75 - 3(6) = 57$.
Line: $\hat{y} = 57 + 3x$.

blocks.title: A prediction too far
blocks.q: The students in that data studied between 2 and 10 hours. What does the line predict for 30 hours, and should you trust it?
steps: The test is out of 100, so the prediction is impossible.
The data only show the pattern between 2 and 10 hours. Beyond that, the line has no support.
blocks.a: 147, which is nonsense: this is extrapolation.

blocks.html: Extrapolation: using the line for x-values far outside the range of the data. The straight-line pattern may bend, level off or stop. Check: is the x you are plugging in between the smallest and largest x in the data?

Because $b = r s_y/s_x$ and $|r| < 1$, a student 1 SD above average in study time is predicted to be only $r$ SDs above average in score. Predictions are pulled toward the mean: this is "regression to the mean." The econometrics course builds on this line in Simple Regression: Fitting a Line.

blocks.html: A least-squares line is only useful if you can say what its numbers mean for the situation. That means two sentences, one for the slope and one for the intercept, each with units and the word "predicted."

Slope $b$: for each one-unit increase in x, the predicted y changes by $b$ (in y's units). Intercept $a$: the predicted y when $x = 0$, which has a real meaning only if $x = 0$ makes sense and is near the data.

The line describes the trend of many individuals, not a rule each one follows. Real points scatter above and below it, so the slope is the change in the average (predicted) y, not a guaranteed change for any one individual. The intercept is just where the line crosses $x = 0$; if no data come from near $x = 0$, it is only an anchor for the line.

blocks.name: stat-chart
blocks.cap: Used cars with the line ŷ = 24 − 1.8x (in thousands of dollars). The cars scatter around the line; none follows it exactly.

blocks.title: Reading a slope
blocks.q: For used cars of one model, $\widehat{\text{price}} = 24{,}000 - 1{,}800 \cdot \text{age}$ (dollars, years). Interpret the slope and the intercept.
steps: Slope $-1{,}800$: for each additional year of age, the predicted price drops by \$1,800.
Intercept $24{,}000$: a brand-new car (age 0) is predicted to cost \$24,000. New cars exist and the data include young cars, so this makes sense.
blocks.a: Each year of age lowers the predicted price by \$1,800; a new one is predicted at \$24,000.

blocks.title: Comparing two individuals
blocks.q: Two cars of this model differ in age by 3 years. How do their predicted prices compare?
steps: Each year changes the prediction by $-1{,}800$.
blocks.a: The older car is predicted to sell for \$5,400 less.

blocks.title: An intercept with no meaning
blocks.q: For adults, $\widehat{\text{weight}} = -180 + 5 \cdot \text{height}$ (pounds, inches). Interpret the intercept.
steps: At height 0 inches the line predicts $-180$ pounds.
No adult is 0 inches tall, and a negative weight is impossible: $x = 0$ is far outside the data.
The intercept only positions the line; it has no meaning here.
blocks.a: It has no real meaning; it just anchors the line.

blocks.html: Stating a predicted change as an exact change for every individual: "every car loses exactly \$1,800 a year." The line describes the average trend; individual cars sit above or below it. Check your sentence for the word "predicted" or "on average."

Slopes always carry units: dollars per year, points per hour. If you cannot name the units, you have not yet said what the slope means. In econometrics, the slope is the start of every "how much does y change with x?" question.

blocks.html: In Algebra 1 you used residuals to judge a line of fit. With the least-squares line they become a powerful check: a plot of the residuals shows whether a line was the right model at all.

The residual of a point is $e = y - \hat{y}$ (actual minus predicted). A residual plot graphs the residuals against x. If a line is a good model, the residuals look like random scatter around 0 with about the same spread everywhere. A curve or a fan shape means the line is missing something.

The least-squares line already removes the straight-line trend, so whatever is left over is what the line could not explain. If that leftover still has a pattern, such as positive at both ends and negative in the middle, the data bend and a straight line systematically misses. A random cloud means there is nothing systematic left for a line to fix.

blocks.title: One residual
blocks.q: The line is $\hat{y} = 57 + 3x$. A student who studied 8 hours scored 85. Find the residual.
steps: Predicted: $\hat{y} = 57 + 3(8) = 81$.
Residual: $85 - 81 = 4$.
Positive: the point lies 4 points above the line.

blocks.name: stat-chart
blocks.cap: Residuals from the least-squares line ŷ = −22 + 11x fitted to y = x². They are positive at both ends and negative in the middle: a clear curve.

blocks.title: Reading a residual plot
blocks.q: For $x = 1, \ldots, 10$ and $y = x^2$, the line has $r \approx 0.97$. Its residual plot is shown above. Is a line a good model?
steps: The residuals form a U: positive, then negative, then positive again.
That pattern means the line is too high in the middle and too low at the ends: the data curve.
So despite the high $r$, a curved model would fit better.
blocks.a: No. The U-shaped residual plot shows the form is curved.

blocks.name: scatter
blocks.cap: The same data with the line and its residuals (green above, red below). Drag points to see how the residuals change.

blocks.html: Taking a high $r$ as proof that a linear model is right. $r$ measures how close the points are to some line; it does not say a line is the right shape. Check the residual plot: any curve or fan means "not linear" no matter how big $r$ is.

blocks.html: A residual plot tells you whether a line is the right shape. The next question is how much the line helps. The answer is $r^2$, the square of the correlation, which has a clear meaning of its own.

$$r^2 = 1 - \dfrac{\text{SSE}}{\text{SST}},$$ where $\text{SST} = \sum (y - \bar{y})^2$ is the variation in y with no model and $\text{SSE} = \sum (y - \hat{y})^2$ is the variation left after the line. $r^2$ is the fraction of the variation in y explained by the linear relationship with x.

Without x, the best single guess for every y is $\bar{y}$, and its total squared error is SST. With the line, the squared error drops to SSE. The fraction removed, $(\text{SST} - \text{SSE})/\text{SST} = 1 - \text{SSE}/\text{SST}$, is how much knowing x helped. For the least-squares line this fraction is exactly the square of $r$ (a fact that follows from the z-score derivation of the line).

blocks.name: scatter
blocks.cap: The squares are the squared residuals (SSE). Make the points line up and watch r² approach 1.

blocks.title: From r to r²
blocks.q: The correlation between hours of sunlight and plant growth is $r = 0.8$. Interpret $r^2$.
steps: About 64% of the variation in plant growth is explained by the linear relationship with hours of sunlight.
The other 36% comes from other things (water, soil, genetics) and chance.
blocks.a: $r^2 = 0.64$: 64% of the variation in growth is explained.

blocks.title: From sums of squares
blocks.q: For a data set, $\text{SST} = 200$ and $\text{SSE} = 50$. The slope is negative. Find $r^2$ and $r$.
steps: $r = \pm\sqrt{0.75} \approx \pm 0.866$.
r has the same sign as the slope: $r \approx -0.866$.

blocks.html: Reading $r^2 = 0.64$ as "64% of the points are on the line" or "predictions are right 64% of the time." $r^2$ is about variation in y, not about individual points. Check your sentence: it should say "of the variation in [y] is explained by the linear relationship with [x]."
Squaring hides the sign: $r = 0.8$ and $r = -0.8$ both give $r^2 = 0.64$. To recover r from $r^2$, take the square root and use the sign of the slope.

blocks.html: The least-squares line minimizes squared residuals, and squaring makes big misses very costly. So a single unusual point can drag the whole line toward itself. This lesson sorts unusual points by what they do to the line and to $r$ and $r^2$.

An outlier has a large residual (it is far from the line in the y-direction). A high-leverage point has an x-value far from the others. A point is influential if removing it changes the slope (or the whole line) a lot. High-leverage points that do not follow the pattern are usually the influential ones.

Think of the line as a seesaw balanced at $(\bar{x}, \bar{y})$. A point near the middle of the x-values pushes near the pivot: it can lift the line a little but cannot tilt it much. A point far out in x pushes at the end of a long lever, so if it sits off the pattern it can tilt the line a lot. A far-out point that lies right on the pattern agrees with the line, so it changes little (it even makes $r$ look stronger).

blocks.name: scatter
blocks.cap: Drag the point at x = 12 up and down. It swings the line around. Then drag it to x = 3 and do the same: the line barely tilts.

blocks.title: Measuring influence
blocks.q: Five points $(1, 2), (2, 4), (3, 5), (4, 4), (5, 6)$ have least-squares slope $0.8$ and $r \approx 0.85$. Adding $P = (12, 2)$ changes the slope to about $-0.11$ and $r$ to about $-0.27$. Describe P.
steps: P has x = 12, far beyond the other x-values (1 to 5): high leverage.
It falls far below where the pattern predicts ($1.8 + 0.8 \cdot 12 = 11.4$).
Including it flips the slope from positive to slightly negative: it is very influential.
blocks.a: P is a high-leverage, influential point.

blocks.title: An outlier with little influence
blocks.q: Instead, add $(3, 12)$ to the five points. The slope stays $0.8$ and $r$ drops to about $0.33$. Describe this point.
steps: Its x-value, 3, is the mean of the x-values: no leverage at all.
It is far above the line: a large residual, so it is an outlier.
It lifts the line (the intercept rises from 1.8 to 3.1) but cannot tilt it, and it weakens $r$ a lot.
blocks.a: An outlier, but not influential on the slope.

blocks.html: Report what you find with and without an influential point, and look for a reason: a typing error, a different kind of individual, or a real but rare case. Do not quietly delete points you dislike.

Assuming every outlier is influential, or that a point is harmless because its residual is small. An influential point pulls the line toward itself, so its own residual can look small. Check by refitting without the point and comparing slopes.

blocks.html: When a residual plot shows a curve, a line is the wrong model. For two common curves, exponential growth and power laws, the properties of logarithms turn the curve into a straight line, and then everything you know about lines applies.

Exponential $y = a \cdot b^x$ becomes $\log y = \log a + (\log b)x$: plot $\log y$ against $x$. Power $y = a \cdot x^p$ becomes $\log y = \log a + p \log x$: plot $\log y$ against $\log x$. Fit a least-squares line to the straightened data, then undo the logs.

Logs turn products into sums and powers into multiples: $\log(a \cdot b^x) = \log a + x \log b$. Exponential growth multiplies y by the same factor $b$ for each step in x; after taking logs, that becomes adding the same amount $\log b$ each step, which is exactly what a straight line does.

blocks.cap: Bacteria doubling every hour: a curve.

blocks.name: stat-chart
blocks.cap: The same data after taking log y: a straight line with slope log 2 ≈ 0.301.

blocks.title: Straightening exponential data
blocks.q: Bacteria counts (thousands) are 3, 6, 12, 24, 48 at hours 0 to 4. Show that $(x, \log y)$ is linear and find the model.
steps: The logs are $0.477, 0.778, 1.079, 1.380, 1.681$; they go up by $0.301$ each hour, so $(x, \log y)$ is a line.
The line: $\log \hat{y} = 0.477 + 0.301x$.

blocks.title: Predicting from a log model
blocks.q: A fitted line is $\log \hat{y} = 0.5 + 0.25x$. Predict y at $x = 6$.

blocks.title: A power model
blocks.q: For animals, a log-log fit gives $\log \hat{y} = 0.301 + 2\log x$. Write the model.
steps: Undo the log: $\hat{y} = 10^{0.301} \cdot 10^{2 \log x} = 2 \cdot x^2$.
Check: $10^{0.301} \approx 2$ because $\log 2 \approx 0.301$.

blocks.html: After straightening, check the residual plot of the transformed data. If it is random scatter, the model fits; if it still curves, try the other transformation.
Forgetting to undo the log. The line predicts $\log y$, not $y$: if $\log \hat{y} = 2$, the prediction is $10^2 = 100$, not 2. Check that your prediction is in the original units.

blocks.html: A strong correlation is tempting to read as cause and effect. You saw in Algebra 1 that correlation is not causation. Here we name the ways an association can arise without one variable causing the other.

An association between x and y can come from (1) x causing y, (2) y causing x, (3) a lurking variable that affects both, or (4) chance. Observational data alone cannot tell these apart. A well-designed randomized experiment can.

If a third variable pushes both x and y up and down, x and y move together even though neither touches the other. On hot days, people buy more ice cream and also spend more time in the sun, so ice cream sales and sunburns rise together. Banning ice cream would not prevent a single sunburn. Random assignment breaks this link: it gives the treatment without regard to temperature or anything else, so the lurking variable ends up balanced between the groups.

blocks.name: stat-chart
blocks.cap: Daily ice cream sales and sunburn cases at a beach town: a strong positive association, driven by the weather.

blocks.title: Finding the lurking variable
blocks.q: Among children ages 5 to 12, shoe size and reading score are strongly correlated. Do bigger feet improve reading?
steps: Ask what could affect both variables.
Older children have bigger feet, and older children have had more years of reading practice.
Age is a lurking variable. Among children of the same age, the association would mostly vanish.

blocks.title: Which way does it run?
blocks.q: Cities with more police officers have more crime. Do police cause crime?
steps: Reverse cause is likely: cities with more crime hire more police.
City size is also a lurking variable: big cities have more of both.
blocks.a: No. The association likely runs the other way, and size affects both.

blocks.html: Concluding that one variable causes the other from a correlation alone, such as "ice cream causes drownings" because both rise in summer. Check by asking: what else changes along with x? Could y cause x? Was x assigned at random?

Correlation is still useful. You can predict sunburn risk from ice cream sales even though one does not cause the other. Prediction needs association; changing outcomes needs cause. Telling these apart is the central problem of causal inference in econometrics.

blocks.html: In Grade 7 you saw that a random sample gives every member of a population a fair chance to be chosen. Asking every member (a census) is usually too slow or too costly, so we study a sample and use it to learn about the whole population. How the sample is chosen decides whether that works.

The population is the whole group we want to learn about; a parameter is a number describing it (like the true proportion $p$). A sample is the part we observe; a statistic is a number computed from it (like $\hat{p}$). Random designs: simple random sample (every group of size n equally likely), stratified (split into similar groups, then sample randomly within each), cluster (randomly choose whole groups and take everyone in them), systematic (a random start, then every kth one).

Chance is fair in a way people are not. When a person picks "typical" individuals, their choices lean toward whoever is easy to reach or seems interesting. A random method cannot play favorites, so on average its samples look like the population. And because the randomness is planned, we can calculate how much sample results vary, which is the key to every margin of error later in the course.

blocks.title: Naming the design
blocks.q: A principal wants 80 of the school's 1,200 students. Plan A: number all students and let a computer pick 80. Plan B: pick 20 at random from each grade, 9 through 12. Plan C: pick 3 homerooms at random and survey everyone in them. Name each design.
steps: Plan A: every set of 80 students is equally likely, so it is a simple random sample.
Plan B: the population is split by grade (strata) and each grade is sampled: stratified.
Plan C: whole homerooms (clusters) are chosen, and everyone in them is surveyed: cluster.
blocks.a: A is simple random, B is stratified, C is cluster.

blocks.title: A systematic sample
blocks.q: A list has 1,500 customers and you want 60. How do you take a systematic sample?
steps: Spread the picks evenly: $1{,}500 \div 60 = 25$.
Choose a random starting number from 1 to 25, say 7, then take customers 7, 32, 57, and so on.
blocks.a: Take every 25th customer after a random start.

blocks.name: sampling
blocks.cap: Each random sample gives a slightly different mean. Random sampling makes that variation predictable: the sample means center on the population mean.

blocks.html: Thinking a convenience sample is random because the people were not chosen on purpose. "The first 50 people at the mall entrance" uses no chance at all; those people share where and when they shop. Check: could you write down how chance picked each member?

blocks.html: A random sampling method aims at the truth. A biased method aims somewhere else, and it misses in the same direction every time you use it. This lesson names the usual ways surveys go wrong.

Bias is a systematic error from the way data are collected. Common sources: undercoverage (some groups cannot be chosen), nonresponse (chosen people do not answer), voluntary response (people choose themselves, usually those with strong opinions), convenience sampling, and response bias (leading questions, sensitive topics, interviewer effects). A bigger sample does not reduce bias.

Picture throwing darts. Variability is how scattered the darts are; bias is how far the center of the cluster is from the bull's-eye. Taking a larger random sample tightens the cluster, but if the method aims at the wrong spot, a tight cluster in the wrong spot is still wrong, and now it looks convincing. Only a better method moves the aim.

blocks.title: Naming the bias
blocks.q: A city council wants to know whether residents support a new dog park. It posts a link on the city's pet-adoption page asking visitors to vote. Of 900 votes, 88% say yes. What is the problem?
steps: People chose whether to respond: voluntary response.
The link was on a pet page, so dog owners were far more likely to see it: undercoverage of everyone else.
Both push the result toward "yes," so 88% probably overstates support.
blocks.a: Voluntary response and undercoverage; the estimate is likely too high.

blocks.title: Question wording
blocks.q: Compare: "Do you support the new library?" with "Do you support raising your taxes to build a new library?" Why might the results differ?
steps: The second version reminds people of a cost, the first does not.
Changing the wording changes the answers people give: response bias.
A fair survey uses neutral wording and the same question for everyone.
blocks.a: The wording itself changes the responses.

blocks.title: Size does not fix bias
blocks.q: In 1936 a magazine mailed millions of ballots, mostly to people listed as car owners and telephone subscribers, and about 2.4 million came back predicting a clear win for Alf Landon. Franklin Roosevelt won in a landslide. Why did such a huge sample fail?
steps: In 1936 car and telephone owners were wealthier than voters overall: undercoverage.
Only a fraction of those mailed answered: nonresponse.
Millions of biased answers give a very precise estimate of the wrong number.
blocks.a: The method was biased; size could not save it.

blocks.html: Believing that a larger sample fixes a biased sampling method. More responses collected the same way repeat the same bias. Check the method first: who could be chosen, who answered, and how the question was worded.

blocks.name: sampling
blocks.cap: With a fair random method, larger samples (slide n up) cluster more tightly around the true mean. That is variability shrinking. A biased method would cluster tightly around the wrong value.

blocks.html: Surveys describe a population; many questions are about causes. Does a new medicine work? Does sleep improve test scores? You know that association does not prove cause and that how data are collected decides what they can tell you. Two kinds of study answer cause questions very differently.

In an observational study, researchers observe and measure but do not influence the subjects. In an experiment, researchers deliberately impose a treatment on the subjects (ideally by random assignment) and measure the response. Only a well-designed randomized experiment can show cause and effect.

In an observational study, people choose their own "treatment," and people who choose differently tend to differ in other ways too. Coffee drinkers may also sleep less, smoke more or work longer hours. Those confounding variables are mixed up with the treatment, so any difference could come from them. Random assignment makes the groups alike, on average, in every other way, measured or not, so a clear difference in response can be pinned on the treatment.

blocks.title: Which kind of study?
blocks.q: Researchers compare the heart health of 5,000 adults who drink coffee daily with adults who do not, using medical records. Observational study or experiment?
steps: The adults chose whether to drink coffee; the researchers only looked at records.
Nothing was imposed: it is an observational study.

blocks.title: An experiment
blocks.q: Volunteers are randomly assigned to chew gum or not during a memory test, and the gum group scores higher. Can we say the gum caused the higher scores?
steps: The researchers imposed the treatment (gum), and chance decided who got it: a randomized experiment.
Random assignment balances other influences (sleep, ability, mood) between the groups.
If the difference is too large to be chance, gum is the best explanation.
blocks.a: Yes, for subjects like these volunteers, if the difference is statistically significant.

blocks.title: Spotting confounding
blocks.q: Students who eat breakfast have higher grades than students who skip it (an observational study). Name a possible confounding variable.
steps: Families who make breakfast every day may also keep regular bedtimes and check homework.
Those habits could raise grades on their own, and they travel along with breakfast.
blocks.a: Family routines (for example, sleep habits) are confounded with breakfast.

blocks.html: Drawing a cause-and-effect conclusion from an observational study: "coffee protects your heart." Check the design: if the explanatory variable was not assigned at random, say "is associated with," not "causes."

Experiments are not always possible or ethical (you cannot assign people to smoke). Then researchers use careful observational designs and statistical controls, the subject of causal inference in econometrics.

blocks.html: Knowing that experiments can show cause is only the start. A badly run experiment can still mislead. Four principles turn an experiment into convincing evidence.

Comparison: compare two or more treatments, often including a control group (no treatment or a placebo). Random assignment: use chance to assign subjects to treatments. Replication: use enough subjects in each group that chance differences average out. Blocking (optional): group similar subjects first and randomize within each block. Add blinding when expectations could affect results.

Each principle removes a different way to be fooled. Without comparison, any change might be due to time passing. Without random assignment, the groups might differ from the start. Without replication, one unusual subject could decide the result. Blocking removes a known source of variation (like gender or field location) from the comparison, so a real treatment effect is easier to see. A placebo and blinding stop the act of being treated, or the researcher's hopes, from changing the response.

blocks.title: Designing an experiment
blocks.q: Design an experiment to test whether a new fertilizer increases tomato yield, using 40 plants.
steps: Treatments: new fertilizer versus the usual one (comparison).
Number the plants 1–40 and use a random number generator to pick 20 for the new fertilizer; the other 20 get the usual one (random assignment, replication).
Grow all plants in the same conditions and compare the mean yield of the two groups.
If half the plants are in sun and half in shade, randomize within the sunny plants and within the shady plants separately (blocking).
blocks.a: A randomized comparison of two groups of 20, blocked by location if needed.

blocks.title: Counting treatments
blocks.q: An experiment tests 3 watering levels and 2 kinds of soil, with every combination used. Each treatment gets 5 plants. How many treatments and plants?
steps: Every watering level pairs with every soil: $3 \times 2 = 6$ treatments.
Replication: $6 \times 5 = 30$ plants.

head: Randomly assigned
Not randomly assigned

blocks.cap: What each kind of randomness lets you conclude.

blocks.html: Confusing random sampling with random assignment. Random sampling (choosing who is in the study) lets you generalize to the population. Random assignment (choosing who gets which treatment) lets you conclude cause and effect. Volunteers randomly assigned to diets give causal evidence about volunteers like them, not a statement about all adults. Check which kind of randomness the study used.

blocks.html: News stories, ads and social media posts are full of statistics. You now know enough about sampling and experiments to ask the right questions before believing a claim.

Judge a statistical claim by how the data were produced. Ask: Who was studied, and how were they chosen? Was anything randomly assigned? How many were studied, and how much did results vary? What exactly was measured or asked? Does the conclusion match the design (association versus cause, these subjects versus everyone)?

A number is only as good as the process that made it. A precise-looking "73%" from a self-selected online poll carries less information than a rough "about 60%" from a careful random sample. Most misleading claims are not false arithmetic; they are true numbers attached to the wrong conclusion.

items: Size and variation: could chance explain the result?
Measurement: neutral wording? What was actually counted?
Conclusion: does "causes" or "all Americans" go beyond the design?

blocks.title: A causal headline
blocks.q: A headline reads: "Chess makes kids smarter: chess club members get higher grades." The story compares club members with other students. Evaluate.
steps: Students chose to join the club: an observational study.
Students who join a chess club may already like school and get support at home (confounding).
The data show an association; they do not show that chess causes better grades.
blocks.a: The headline claims cause from an observational comparison.

blocks.title: Relative versus absolute risk
blocks.q: An ad says a medicine "cuts the risk of a side effect in half," from 2 in 10,000 people to 1 in 10,000. Evaluate.
steps: Relative change: from 2 to 1 is indeed half.
Absolute change: 1 fewer case per 10,000 people, or 0.01%.
Both are true, but "in half" sounds far bigger than the actual difference.
blocks.a: A large relative change can be a tiny absolute change; report both.

blocks.html: Trusting a result because the number looks precise or the sample is large. A poll of 50,000 self-selected website visitors is less trustworthy than a random sample of 1,000. Check the design questions first, then the numbers.
Misleading graphs are a cousin of misleading claims: a bar graph whose axis starts at 950 instead of 0 can make a 2% change look like doubling. Read the axis labels.

blocks.html: In Grade 7 you listed sample spaces with lists, tables and trees. Probability rules are built on that idea, plus the language of sets: an event is just a set of outcomes, and "or," "and" and "not" are ways of combining sets.

The sample space $S$ is the set of all possible outcomes. An event is a subset of $S$. Complement $A^{\prime}$ (not A): outcomes not in A. Union $A \cup B$ (A or B): outcomes in A, in B, or in both. Intersection $A \cap B$ (A and B): outcomes in both. When outcomes are equally likely, $$P(A) = \dfrac{\text{number of outcomes in } A}{\text{number of outcomes in } S}.$$

Probability measures how much of the sample space an event covers. If every outcome is equally likely, each outcome carries the same share of probability, so counting outcomes gives the probability. Thinking of events as regions (a Venn diagram) makes "or" and "and" visible: "or" is everything covered by either region, "and" is only the overlap.

blocks.name: venn

opts.task: Roll a die. A = even = {2, 4, 6}, B = greater than 3 = {4, 5, 6}. Shade A ∪ B.

blocks.cap: Each number is how many outcomes of one die roll sit in that region: {2} in A only, {4, 6} in both, {5} in B only, {1, 3} in neither.

blocks.title: One die
blocks.q: Roll a fair die. Let A = "even" and B = "greater than 3." Find $P(A \cup B)$, $P(A \cap B)$ and $P(A^{\prime})$.
steps: $S = \{1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6\}$, six equally likely outcomes. $A = \{2, 4, 6\}$ and $B = \{4, 5, 6\}$.
$A \cup B = \{2, 4, 5, 6\}$: 4 outcomes, so $P = \dfrac{4}{6} = \dfrac{2}{3}$. (4 and 6 are in both, but each is listed once.)

blocks.title: One card
blocks.q: Draw one card from a standard 52-card deck. What is the probability it is a heart or a face card (jack, queen, king)?
steps: Hearts: 13 cards. Face cards: 12 cards (3 in each of 4 suits).
The jack, queen and king of hearts are in both groups, so they were counted twice.
Cards in "heart or face card": $13 + 12 - 3 = 22$.

blocks.html: Reading "A or B" as "exactly one of A and B." In probability, "or" is inclusive: outcomes in both events count too. For the die, $A \cup B$ includes 4 and 6. Check with a Venn diagram: shade both circles completely, overlap included.

blocks.html: Counting the outcomes in "A or B" worked in the last lesson because we could list them. When all we know are the probabilities of A, of B and of both, we need a rule.
$$P(A \cup B) = P(A) + P(B) - P(A \cap B).$$ If A and B are mutually exclusive (they cannot happen together), $P(A \cap B) = 0$ and $P(A \cup B) = P(A) + P(B)$.

Adding $P(A)$ and $P(B)$ adds up the two circles of the Venn diagram. The overlap belongs to both circles, so it is counted twice. Subtracting $P(A \cap B)$ once leaves every outcome counted exactly once. When the circles do not overlap, there is nothing to subtract.

blocks.name: venn
blocks.cap: 120 students: S = plays a sport (45), B = in the band (30), 12 in both. The readout checks the addition rule.

blocks.title: Counts from a survey
blocks.q: Of 120 students, 45 play a sport, 30 are in the band, and 12 do both. What is the probability that a randomly chosen student plays a sport or is in the band?
steps: Add, then remove the double count: $45 + 30 - 12 = 63$ students.

blocks.title: With probabilities
blocks.q: $P(A) = 0.45$, $P(B) = 0.30$, $P(A \cap B) = 0.12$. Find $P(A \cup B)$ and the probability of neither.
steps: "Neither" is the complement of "A or B": $1 - 0.63 = 0.37$.

blocks.title: Mutually exclusive events
blocks.q: A spinner lands on red with probability $0.25$ and on blue with probability $0.4$. It cannot land on both. Find $P(\text{red or blue})$.
steps: Red and blue cannot happen together, so the overlap is 0.

blocks.html: The same idea extends to three events: add the three probabilities, subtract the three pairwise overlaps, then add back the triple overlap, which was removed once too often. This is called inclusion and exclusion.

Adding $P(A) + P(B)$ without subtracting the overlap. Check: a probability can never exceed 1. If $P(A) = 0.7$ and $P(B) = 0.6$, simple adding gives 1.3, which is impossible; the events must overlap by at least 0.3.

blocks.html: New information changes probabilities. If you know a family owns a dog, the chance it also owns a cat is a different question from the chance a random family owns a cat. Conditional probability makes that precise, and it reuses the Venn diagram picture.

The probability of A given B is $$P(A \mid B) = \dfrac{P(A \cap B)}{P(B)},$$ the fraction of B's outcomes that are also in A. With counts: $P(A \mid B) = \frac{\text{number in both}}{\text{number in } B}$.

"Given B" means we now know we are somewhere inside B. Everything outside B is ruled out, so B becomes the new sample space. Within it, the outcomes where A also happens are exactly $A \cap B$. So the new probability is the size of $A \cap B$ compared with the size of B, not with the whole sample space.

blocks.name: venn
blocks.cap: 200 households: D = owns a dog (80), C = owns a cat (50), 20 own both. "C|D" grays out everything outside D.

blocks.title: Counts
blocks.q: Of 200 households, 80 own a dog, 50 own a cat, and 20 own both. A dog-owning household is chosen at random. What is the probability it also owns a cat?
steps: Given "dog," the sample space shrinks to the 80 dog owners.
Of those, 20 also own a cat.
$P(\text{cat} \mid \text{dog}) = \dfrac{20}{80} = \dfrac{1}{4}$.

blocks.title: The other direction
blocks.q: Using the same households, find $P(\text{dog} \mid \text{cat})$.
steps: Given "cat," use only the 50 cat owners.
Of those, 20 own a dog: $\dfrac{20}{50} = \dfrac{2}{5}$.
Same overlap, different condition, different answer: $\frac{1}{4} \ne \frac{2}{5}$.

blocks.title: With probabilities
blocks.q: $P(B) = 0.4$ and $P(A \cap B) = 0.1$. Find $P(A \mid B)$.
steps: Divide the probability of both by the probability of the condition.

blocks.html: Confusing $P(A \mid B)$ with $P(B \mid A)$. The probability that a person who tested positive is sick is not the probability that a sick person tests positive. Check what comes after the bar: that event is the condition, and its total goes in the denominator.

blocks.name: tree
blocks.cap: The second-level branches are conditional probabilities: given the first branch. Multiplying along a path gives P(both).

blocks.html: In Algebra 1 you read two-way tables with row and column percents. Those percents are conditional probabilities: the row or column you restrict to is the condition.

In a two-way table, divide the cell by the total of the condition:
$$P(\text{row} \mid \text{column}) = \dfrac{\text{cell}}{\text{column total}}, \qquad P(\text{column} \mid \text{row}) = \dfrac{\text{cell}}{\text{row total}}.$$
With no condition, divide by the grand total.

A condition picks out one row or one column of the table: those are the only individuals we are now choosing from. The cell where the row and column meet holds the ones that satisfy both. So the denominator is always the total of whatever you were "given."

head: Took review class
Did not
Total
blocks.cap: 200 students who took a certification exam.

blocks.title: Given the column
blocks.q: Find the probability that a student passed, given that the student took the review class.
steps: The condition is "took the review class": use that column, 50 students.
Of those, 45 passed.
$P(\text{passed} \mid \text{review}) = \dfrac{45}{50} = 0.9$.

blocks.title: Given the row
blocks.q: Find the probability that a student took the review class, given that the student passed.
steps: The condition is "passed": use that row, 135 students.
Of those, 45 took the class.
$P(\text{review} \mid \text{passed}) = \dfrac{45}{135} = \dfrac{1}{3}$.

blocks.title: No condition
blocks.q: Find the probability that a randomly chosen student took the review class and passed.
steps: No "given," so all 200 students are in play.

blocks.html: Dividing by the grand total when the question gives a condition. "Of the students who took the review class, what fraction passed?" has 50 in the denominator, not 200. Check: find the word "given" (or "of those who," "among") and divide by that group's total.

Comparing $P(\text{passed} \mid \text{review}) = 0.9$ with $$P(\text{passed} \mid \text{no review}) = 90/150 = 0.6$$ shows an association between the class and passing. (This is observational data, so it does not prove the class causes passing.)

blocks.html: Sometimes knowing B changes the chance of A (as with the review class and passing). Sometimes it changes nothing at all. That second case has a name, and it builds directly on conditional probability.
Events A and B are independent if knowing one happened does not change the probability of the other: $P(A \mid B) = P(A)$. Equivalently, $P(A \cap B) = P(A) \cdot P(B)$. Otherwise they are dependent.

Start from the definition $P(A \mid B) = P(A \cap B)/P(B)$. If $P(A \mid B) = P(A)$, multiply both sides by $P(B)$ to get $P(A \cap B) = P(A)P(B)$; the steps reverse, so the two tests say the same thing. In words: A happens in the same fraction of the B-world as of the whole world.

blocks.name: tree
blocks.cap: Two coin flips: the second flip's branches are 1/2 and 1/2 no matter how the first one landed. That is independence.

blocks.title: Checking a table
blocks.q: Of 200 students, 60 play an instrument. Among the 80 ninth graders, 24 play one. Are "plays an instrument" and "ninth grader" independent?
steps: $P(\text{instrument}) = \dfrac{60}{200} = 0.3$.
$$P(\text{instrument} \mid \text{9th grade}) = \dfrac{24}{80} = 0.3$$
Equal: knowing the grade does not change the chance.

blocks.title: Checking with the product
blocks.q: $P(A) = 0.6$, $P(B) = 0.5$, $P(A \cap B) = 0.2$. Are A and B independent?
steps: If independent, $P(A \cap B)$ would be $0.6 \times 0.5 = 0.3$.

blocks.title: Mutually exclusive is not independent
blocks.q: A = "the die shows 1" and B = "the die shows 6." Are they independent?
steps: They cannot both happen: $P(A \cap B) = 0$, but $P(A)P(B) = \frac{1}{36}$.
Knowing the die shows 1 changes the chance of 6 from $\frac{1}{6}$ to 0.

blocks.html: Thinking mutually exclusive events are independent. They are the opposite: if A happens, B cannot, so knowing about A tells you everything about B. Check: if $P(A \cap B) = 0$ but both $P(A)$ and $P(B)$ are positive, the events are dependent.

blocks.html: The definition of conditional probability can be turned around to find the probability that two things both happen, one after the other. For independent events this is plain multiplication; otherwise the second factor must be conditional.
$$P(A \cap B) = P(A) \cdot P(B \mid A).$$ If A and B are independent, $P(B \mid A) = P(B)$ and this becomes $P(A)P(B)$. On a tree diagram: multiply along the branches of a path.

Multiply both sides of $P(B \mid A) = P(A \cap B)/P(A)$ by $P(A)$. In words: first A must happen, and then, in the world where A happened, B must happen. Drawing without replacement changes the world after the first draw (one fewer of that color, one fewer in total), so the second probability must be the conditional one.

blocks.name: tree
blocks.cap: A bag of 5 red and 3 blue marbles, two draws without replacement. Tap outcomes to add their probabilities.

blocks.title: Without replacement
blocks.q: A bag holds 5 red and 3 blue marbles. Draw two without replacement. Find $P(\text{both red})$.
steps: First draw: $P(\text{red}) = \dfrac{5}{8}$.
Given a red is gone: 4 red of 7 left, $P(\text{red} \mid \text{red}) = \dfrac{4}{7}$.
Multiply: $\dfrac{5}{8} \cdot \dfrac{4}{7} = \dfrac{20}{56} = \dfrac{5}{14}$.

blocks.title: With replacement
blocks.q: Same bag, but the first marble is put back before the second draw. Find $P(\text{both red})$.
steps: Replacing the marble restores the bag, so the draws are independent.
$\dfrac{5}{8} \cdot \dfrac{5}{8} = \dfrac{25}{64}$.

blocks.title: At least one
blocks.q: Without replacement, find the probability that at least one of the two marbles is blue.
steps: "At least one blue" is the complement of "both red."
Check with the tree: $\frac{15}{56} + \frac{15}{56} + \frac{6}{56} = \frac{36}{56} = \frac{9}{14}$.

blocks.html: The rule chains: $$P(A \cap B \cap C) = P(A)\,P(B \mid A)\,P(C \mid A \cap B)$$ Three reds in a row from the same bag: $\frac{5}{8} \cdot \frac{4}{7} \cdot \frac{3}{6} = \frac{5}{28}$.

Multiplying unconditional probabilities when drawing without replacement: $\frac{5}{8} \cdot \frac{5}{8}$ for two reds. After the first red is gone, the bag has changed. Check: write down what is left in the bag before each draw.

blocks.html: A medical test is "90% accurate," and you test positive. How likely is it that you have the condition? Most people guess about 90%. The right answer is often far lower. Bayes' rule reverses a conditional probability, using the multiplication rule and the table idea together.

To reverse a conditional probability, imagine a large group (say 10,000 people) and count. In symbols, $$P(D \mid +) = \dfrac{P(D)\,P(+ \mid D)}{P(D)\,P(+ \mid D) + P(D^{\prime})\,P(+ \mid D^{\prime})}.$$ The answer depends heavily on the base rate $P(D)$.

By definition, $P(D \mid +) = P(D \cap +)/P(+)$. The multiplication rule gives the numerator: $P(D \cap +) = P(D)P(+ \mid D)$. A positive test happens in two ways, a true positive or a false positive, so $P(+)$ is the sum of the two paths in the tree (the law of total probability). When the condition is rare, the healthy group is huge, and even a small false-positive rate applied to it produces more positives than the small sick group does.

blocks.name: stat-icons
blocks.cap: Each square is one person. Red: has the condition. Gold: a false alarm. Slide the base rate up and watch the share of real positives grow.

blocks.title: Natural frequencies
blocks.q: A condition affects 1% of people. A test is positive for 90% of people who have it and for 9% of people who do not. You test positive. Find $P(\text{condition} \mid +)$.
steps: Imagine 10,000 people: 100 have the condition, 9,900 do not.
True positives: 90% of 100 = 90.
False positives: 9% of 9,900 = 891.
Positives in all: $90 + 891 = 981$. Of these, 90 have the condition.
$$P(\text{condition} \mid +) = \dfrac{90}{981} \approx 0.092$$

blocks.title: The same answer with the formula
blocks.q: Check the result with Bayes' rule.
steps: Numerator: $$P(D)P(+ \mid D) = 0.01 \times 0.9 = 0.009$$

blocks.title: A second positive test
blocks.q: A person who tested positive takes a second, independent test of the same kind, and it is positive too. Now what is the probability of the condition?
steps: After the first test, the person's probability is $\frac{90}{981} \approx 9.2\%$: that is the new base rate.
Imagine 981 such people: 90 have it, 891 do not.
Second test: true positives $0.9 \times 90 = 81$; false positives $0.09 \times 891 = 80.19$.
blocks.a: About 50%: each positive test raises the probability, starting from the base rate.

blocks.name: tree
blocks.cap: The condition is "Positive" on either path. P(condition | positive) = the selected path divided by both positive paths.

blocks.html: Ignoring how rare the condition is and trusting a positive result too much: treating $P(+ \mid D) = 90\%$ as if it were $P(D \mid +)$. Check by imagining 10,000 people and counting both kinds of positives. If the healthy group is huge, false positives can outnumber true ones.

blocks.html: Probability with equally likely outcomes needs counts, and listing every outcome (as with trees and tables) stops being practical quickly. Counting rules do the listing for you. The first is for arrangements, where order matters.

Multiplication principle: if a task has steps with $n_1, n_2, \ldots$ choices, there are $n_1 \cdot n_2 \cdots$ ways to do it. Arranging $n$ different objects in a row: $n! = n(n-1)\cdots 2 \cdot 1$ ways. Arranging $r$ of $n$ different objects in order: $$_{n}P_{r} = n(n-1)\cdots(n - r + 1) = \dfrac{n!}{(n-r)!}.$$

Fill the positions one at a time. The first position can hold any of the $n$ objects. Whichever you chose, $n - 1$ remain for the second position, and so on. Every first choice combines with every second choice, which is why the counts multiply; a tree diagram shows the branches multiplying. For $_nP_r$ you stop after $r$ positions, which is $n!$ with the unused tail $(n - r)!$ divided away. (By convention $0! = 1$, so $_nP_n = n!$.)

blocks.name: tree
blocks.cap: Arranging A, B and C: 3 choices, then 2, then 1, for 3! = 6 arrangements, each with probability 1/6 if the order is random.

blocks.title: A full arrangement
blocks.q: In how many orders can 5 different books stand on a shelf?
steps: 5 choices for the first spot, 4 for the second, 3, 2, then 1.
$5! = 5 \cdot 4 \cdot 3 \cdot 2 \cdot 1 = 120$.

blocks.title: Some of the objects, in order
blocks.q: A club of 10 elects a president, a vice president and a secretary (different people). How many outcomes are possible?
steps: Order matters: being president is different from being secretary.

blocks.title: Repeated letters
blocks.q: How many different arrangements of the letters in LEVEL are there?
steps: If all 5 letters were different: $5! = 120$.
But the two Ls can swap without changing the word, and so can the two Es: each word was counted $2! \cdot 2! = 4$ times.

blocks.html: Using a permutation when order does not matter. Choosing 3 people for a committee is not like electing three officers: the committee {Ann, Ben, Cal} is one group however you list it, but $_{10}P_3$ counts it 6 times. Check: if you swap two of the chosen, is it a different outcome? If not, see combinations.

Common Core State Standards for Mathematics, S-CP.B.9 (Use permutations and combinations to compute probabilities)

blocks.html: A permutation counts ordered arrangements. Many questions only care which objects are chosen: a committee, a hand of cards, pizza toppings. Then we count each group once.

The number of ways to choose $r$ objects from $n$ different objects, when order does not matter, is
$$\binom{n}{r} = {_nC_r} = \dfrac{_nP_r}{r!} = \dfrac{n!}{r!\,(n-r)!}.$$

Count the ordered choices first: $_nP_r$. Each unordered group of $r$ objects shows up in that count once for every way of ordering it, which is $r!$ times. Dividing by $r!$ leaves each group counted exactly once. Choosing which $r$ to take is the same as choosing which $n - r$ to leave, so $\binom{n}{r} = \binom{n}{n-r}$.

blocks.title: A committee
blocks.q: In how many ways can a committee of 3 be chosen from 10 people?
steps: Ordered choices: $_{10}P_3 = 10 \cdot 9 \cdot 8 = 720$.
Each committee appears in $3! = 6$ orders.

blocks.title: Two groups at once
blocks.q: Choose 2 juniors from 6 and 3 seniors from 5. How many ways?
steps: Juniors: $\binom{6}{2} = 15$. Seniors: $\binom{5}{3} = 10$.
Every junior pair goes with every senior trio: $15 \times 10 = 150$.

blocks.title: At least one
blocks.q: A class of 10 includes 3 chess players. How many teams of 4 include at least one chess player?
steps: All teams: $\binom{10}{4} = 210$.
Teams with no chess players (choose from the other 7): $\binom{7}{4} = 35$.
At least one = all − none: $210 - 35 = 175$.

blocks.html: Deciding "order matters" from the wording "first, second..." alone. Ask what makes two outcomes different. Three officers with different jobs: order matters. Three people getting identical prizes: it does not. Check by swapping two chosen people: a new outcome means permutation; the same outcome means combination.
The numbers $\binom{n}{r}$ are the entries of Pascal's triangle and the coefficients in the binomial theorem. They will reappear in the binomial distribution.
